question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic predicated of God or otherwise related to God; if so, in what relation (God as the one who bears it, acts, gives it, or is its object)? Record the relation, or record that it is not related to God here.

sample.text: **[CHAR-21]** E — The 64-verse corpus reveals God's character across four dimensions. (1) *God as the one who hates perversity*: Pro 8:13 — "pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate" — wisdom (personified as God's attribute) explicitly names hatred of perversity; (2) *God as the one who watches over the perversion of judgment*: Exo 23:8; Deu 16:19 — bribery blinds the wise and subverts the righteous; God's justice is the standard against which the perversion of justice is measured; (3) *God as the one who judges perversity*: Pro 21:12 — "The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin"; Rev 19:2 — "he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality"; (4) *God as the one who disciplines rather than abandons the inwardly twisted*: 2Sa 7:14 — "when he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men... not take my steadfast love from him" — God's response to perversity-as-iniquity is corrective discipline within sustained love rather than abandonment.

Across all sub-groups, the cluster's vocabulary is uniformly negative in the divine portrait — none of the M20 characteristics are attributed to God. Instead, each sub-group reveals God's character as the structural opposite: attentive care (against anxiety), faithful forward-orientation (against despair), inexhaustible mercy (against discouragement), single-minded generosity (against indecision).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Evil as constitutional inner nature is definitionally opposed to God's nature rather than derived from it. Rom 9:14 (vc=65872 — VCG-06) poses and immediately rejects the charge of unrighteousness (adikia) against God — divine sovereign choice is explicitly not constitutionally evil. The verse establishes that God's nature is the structural antithesis of constitutional inner evil. Rom 12:9 (vc=14417 — VCG-06) commands the community to "abhor what is evil" — this command reflects the divine moral character that stands against evil as constitutional nature. 1Cor 13:6 (vc=14341 — VCG-06) frames love (the divine character) as refusing to "rejoice at wrongdoing" — unrighteousness is what love's opposite produces. The evidence collectively reveals God as constitutionally righteous and the human constitutional evil as an inversion of that righteousness.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The three mechanisms reveal God's character through contrast and implication. (1) *God as the one who does not entice through desire*: Jam 1:14 — "each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire" — the verse is set within a context (Jam 1:13 — not quoted but implied) that explicitly distinguishes God from the enticement mechanism: God does not entice toward evil. The mechanism of desire-enticement is constitutively not-God's mode of operation. (2) *God as the ground of covenantal identity*: Act 21:21 — the apostasy charge describes forsaking Moses — the covenantal framework given through Moses is the gift of God's self-revelation; forsaking that covenantal identity is a defection from what God established. (3) *God as the one whose image requires authenticity*: Gal 2:13 — sunupokrinomai (collective hypocrisy) falsifies identity and corrupts community integrity; authenticity before God and in community is what the characteristic destroys.

The anxiety-faculty is shown as the capacity for directed attentive concern — the inner ability to fix attention on something of value and be troubled by its welfare. 1Pe 5:7 reveals God's character most directly in relation to this: "he cares for you" (merimna cast onto God) — the command to transfer anxiety is grounded in God's active, attentive care. The same term (merimna) that names human anxiety about valued things names God's disposition toward the human person. This suggests the anxiety-faculty at its root images God's caring attentiveness — anxiety is the misdirected form of a faculty whose proper direction is the same as God's own orientation toward what he values.

question_text: Does this verse state any purpose, role, or effect the characteristic serves in the person — what it leads the person to be, do, or become? Record it if stated; otherwise record none.

sample.text: Reproach does not serve a created purpose in the sense of a positive inner capacity. It is a condition imposed from outside — the experience of being an object of public contempt and shame. Unlike righteous hatred or abhorrence, there is no commanded righteous reproach. Reproach is what happens to the person, not what they exercise.
distazō and dipsuchos do not surface a created-purpose positive register. Double-mindedness and situational doubt are not presented as created faculties with positive purposes.

**[CHAR-20]** S — The corpus provides no evidence of any positive created purpose for faithlessness. The characteristic is entirely a fallen-condition category: the breaking of the very covenant bonds that the human person was designed to inhabit and maintain. No verse presents unfaithfulness as a designed feature of the image-bearer.

The verse evidence addresses contrition's purpose in the fallen condition clearly — it is the inner posture that positions the person to receive divine revival, nearness, and salvation (Isa 57:15, Psa 34:18). Whether contrition serves a purpose in the pre-fall created design is not addressed. The vocabulary (crushing, breaking, bruising) presupposes a condition requiring restoration — a post-fall frame. The question of whether contrition is a designed feature of creatureliness or a response to the fallen condition is not resolved by the data. OBS-030-045, OBS-030-046, OBS-030-048.

**[CHAR-21]** S — The corpus provides no evidence of any positive created purpose for perversion-as-inner-inversion. The characteristic is entirely a fallen-condition reality: the twisting of what was created straight and good. No verse presents moral perversity as a designed feature.

question_text: Across the evidence, does the characteristic's role read as belonging to created design, to the fallen condition, to both, or as not determinable?

sample.text: The inner-closure pattern is a response to the fallen condition, produced by material prosperity in the absence of the tethering-to-God that right creation would sustain. Deu 32:15 names the pattern as failure (forsook God, scoffed at the Rock) — it presupposes a prior right relationship that is then broken by satiation. Not original design; a fallen pattern.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The corpus strongly evidences contrition as a response to the fallen condition rather than part of original design. Both verses operate in the context of moral failure, limitation, and the recognition of one's true standing before God's holiness: Psa34:18 — "the brokenhearted" and "crushed in spirit" — language that presupposes a condition of inner breaking. Isa57:15 — "contrite" paired with "lowly" — the characteristic arises from genuine confrontation with failure or with divine holiness. There is no evidence in this corpus that contrition exists in the absence of the moral condition (failure, sin, guilt) that occasions it. The characteristic appears structurally responsive to the fallen condition: it is the right inner response to one's own moral reality before a holy God.
Response to fallen condition — both distazō and dipsuchos are failures of trust and commitment that would not arise if the person related to God with complete, undivided trust from the beginning.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence consistently positions wickedness-as-settled-person-identity as a condition of the fallen human, not the original created design. The proverb "out of the wicked comes wickedness" (1Sa 24:13 — vc=42648) treats wickedness as an inner source from which corresponding actions inevitably flow, but without attributing this orientation to original design. Eze 18:20–27 (M10b-A-VCG-07) addresses wickedness as a volitional orientation the will has taken and can reverse — its reversibility implies it is not constitutionally fixed by creation. The question of how wickedness entered the inner person is not directly addressed in this corpus (that belongs to M10/sin-act clusters); what is evidenced is the condition in its settled form. The corpus addresses the wicked person as an existing type, not as an explanation of human origins.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Entirely a response to the fallen condition. Eze 28:15 — "you were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you" — the cherub's pre-fallen blamelessness establishes that injustice was not original to the created being; it was "found in" the being as an emergence from within, not as a design-feature. Eze 18:24 — "when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice" — injustice enters when the person turns from the prior righteousness; the turn is from, not toward, the designed state.

question_text: Across the evidence, is there any orientation toward a future fullness — something the person moves toward, not only what they currently are? Record it, or record none.

sample.text: **[CLUSTER]** E — All six evidence eschatological orientation, but with strikingly different densities. Char 1 has the highest promise-density in the entire cluster: the shame-removal corpus (Isa 54:4; 61:7; Joe 2:26-27; Zep 3:19; Isa 45:17) makes felt shame the M07 characteristic Scripture most explicitly promises to resolve. Char 5 has the paradigmatic reversal statement: Act 4:11 (rejected stone becoming the cornerstone) is the eschatological reversal of contempt-shame in its most compressed form. Char 2's eschatological horizon is the Day-of-the-Lord completion (all pride finally brought low) and 1Cor 15:43 (mortal dishonour raised in glory). Chars 3 and 5 share the trajectory of the world's false worth-assignments and contempt-verdicts being overturned at God's final word. Char 4's eschatological horizon is Rev 16:15 — conscience-vigilance oriented toward Christ's coming. Char 6's eschatological trajectory is through the Psa 73 lament — maintained innocence vindicated in the sanctuary, pointing toward final vindication. Cluster-level observation: eschatological promise-density is concentrated where suffering is most acutely personal (Chars 1 and 5). The eschatological resolution is most explicitly directed at the most personally felt wounds.
1Cor 2:7 (VCG07 context): "a secret and hidden wisdom of God decreed before the ages for our glory" — wisdom's eschatological destination is glory. The wisdom now received anticipates fullness.

M01-C's terror-as-weapon material includes the eschatological stripping of imperial terror in Sheol (Eze 32:23 corpus) — suggesting the fullness is a world free of terror-as-domination. M01-D's commanded-against-dismay material (Jer 30:10 anchor: "salvation and quiet rest" as the antidote) points toward a state of inner composure as the eschatological goal.

Yes. Eph 2:7 names the eschatological horizon explicitly: "in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" — grace has a future display that exceeds its present form. Eze 20:40–41 in ra.tsah group 795-001 names eschatological acceptance: "there I will accept them" — the divine pleasure as a future fullness of restored relationship. Ba.rakh group 1299-001 carries the Abrahamic blessing extending to "all the families of the earth" (Gen 12:3; 22:18) — a universally-scoped future. The grace-characteristic is oriented toward a future in which what is now partially received is fully displayed.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes: (1) **Psa 16:11** — "at your right hand are pleasures forevermore" — the clearest eschatological statement for Pleasure in the corpus: pleasures in God's presence as a permanent eschatological reality; (2) **Eze 20:41** — "as a pleasing aroma I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you" — future divine acceptance-as-pleasantness as the eschatological restoration goal; (3) **Zec 8:19** — former fasts becoming "cheerful feasts" — the transformation of mourning into Pleasure as eschatological reversal; (4) **Job 36:11** — "if they listen and serve him, they complete their days in pleasantness" — pleasantness as the fruit of faithful obedience with eschatological overtones; (5) **Psa 36:8** — river of delights as the eternal supply in God's house, pointing toward the New Jerusalem's river of life.

question_text: From the characteristic's God-relation (T0.1) and its role (T0.2), what aspect of the divine likeness, if any, does it instantiate in the person? Record the aspect, or record none.

sample.text: **[CHAR-17]** E — Guilt-as-inner-state expresses the image through the image-bearer's *moral accountability before God*: only a being made in God's image stands before God in a morally accountable relationship. Ezr 9:15 — "we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this" — the guilt is experienced as a barrier to standing before God; only a being designed to stand before God (the image-bearer) experiences this specific form of conscience-burden. Gen 42:21 — the brothers' conscience connects past cruelty to present suffering, demonstrating the moral-causal awareness that belongs to the image-bearing conscience.

M46-C expresses the divine image in the capacity to receive and steward material goods as gifts from God with righteousness. The righteous person whose house contains wealth alongside enduring righteousness (Psa 112:3) instantiates the divine character in which abundance and moral integrity coexist. This is image-bearing in the economic domain.

The goodness characteristic expresses the image through the capacity for moral evaluation and alignment with what is genuinely good. 1Ki 8:18 — God affirms David's heart-goodness — shows that the inner moral quality is recognisable to God and reflects his evaluative character. The person whose heart is genuinely good is imaging the divine evaluator. Pro 17:22 (the glad/good heart as good medicine) suggests the image is not merely formal but vital — the good inner state produces healing, which images the divine generativity of goodness.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six characteristics express the divine image through different moral faculties. Char 1 expresses it through the moral consciousness that can register shame — the image-bearer's capacity for self-assessment before the holy. Char 2 expresses it through the moral standing that can be exalted or abased — the reality of the image-bearer's standing before God. Char 3 expresses it through the worth-recognition capacity — the ability to see and honour genuine worth in others as God does. Char 4 expresses it through the conscience's moral-evaluative operation — the creaturely registration of God's moral character. Char 5 expresses it indirectly: the fact that contempt wounds presupposes the person has genuine worth rooted in the image. Char 6 expresses the image most directly through the positive moral faculty — the blameless will and clean conscience that mirror God's own moral purity in creaturely form. Cluster-level pattern: M07's expression of the divine image is concentrated in the moral dimensions — conscience, will, and the capacity for moral self-assessment and accountability before God.

**[E — Condemnation]** The human capacity for moral condemnation — recognising guilt, calling wrong "wrong" — images the divine capacity for just judgment. When the Ninevites condemn the generation that rejected greater light (Mat 12:41, VSG 4846-001), they instantiate the divine image in its judicial aspect: the recognition that moral distinctions are real and that failing to respond to moral truth carries consequences.

question_text: Across the evidence, is the characteristic shared between God and the person, or an exclusively creaturely analogue to something in God?

sample.text: Shared at the evaluative level: tov is used for divine goodness (Psa 119:68 — "you are good and do good," via the goodness registry data) and human goodness (1Ki 8:18). The sharing is real; the asymmetry is constitutive — God's goodness is the standard against which human goodness is measured.

The evidence across sub-groups consistently supports participatory sharing rather than mere analogy. The giving-structure (God gives wisdom: Jam 1:5; God places understanding: Job 38:36; Christ opens minds: Luk 24:45; God gives knowledge: Dan 2:21) shows divine attributes genuinely entering the human person, not merely being resembled. The human characteristic is a real participation in the divine, scaled to the creaturely constitution.
Not shared. Malice has no divine form.
The M20 forms (despair, discouragement, doubt) are exclusively creaturely — arising from finitude and fallenness with no divine counterpart.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Partially shared through the Son's Incarnation, not directly shared in the Father's mode. Heb5:8 and Rom5:19 evidence that the characteristic is genuinely present in the Son — not merely a creaturely analogue but the Son's own enacted posture in the Incarnation. However, the Father's possession of the characteristic in the same form is not evidenced — the Father is the authority to whom submission runs, not the one who submits. The characteristic is thus shared with the person of the Son in his incarnate mode, and is a creaturely analogue to the divine-Son relation with the Father, which the Incarnation makes directly accessible as a pattern for human submission.

question_text: Where the characteristic is present or absent in a person, what does that indicate about the condition of the divine image in them — or is no such indication evidenced?

**[CHAR-21]** E — The presence of perversion reveals the image in its *internally distorted condition*: the faculties that were designed for moral alignment have been twisted against their grain. 1Ti 6:5 — "depraved in mind and deprived of the truth" — the mind (the image's cognitive faculty) has been corrupted at its very seat of understanding. Eph 4:22 — "old self... corrupt through deceitful desires" — the desire-faculty of the image has been turned into the agent of the corruption. The image is not destroyed but its inner faculties (mind, will, heart, desire, speech) are bent away from the moral order they were designed to instantiate.
VCG06 (Pro 26:12 anchor): self-attributed wisdom reveals the divine image occupied by a self-constructed substitute — the image's wisdom-capacity inverted toward self rather than toward God.

Presence = functioning comforter-community; absence = the Lamentations condition: "she has none to comfort her" (Lam 1:2, 1:9, 1:16, 1:17, 1:21 — Group 1741) — the nadir of communal failure. Absence of comforters signals the complete collapse of the community's care-giving capacity.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Political revolt reveals the divine image in a condition of broken covenantal loyalty. 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day" — the ongoing rebellion names a condition in which the image-bearing community refuses the authority structure that God established. 2Ch 21:10's causal chain reveals the deepest dimension: the image-condition that produces political revolt is first a condition of having forsaken the Lord — the vertical loyalty broken before the horizontal political loyalty fractures. Political revolt is thus a surface manifestation of a deeper image-condition of broken loyalty, both toward God and toward his established order.

question_text: Does this verse use the characteristic typologically — pointing beyond the immediate to a covenantal, eschatological, or christological reality; if so, which, and in which direction (the divine instance establishing the pattern, or the human pointing toward the divine)? Record the use and direction, or record none.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in specific registers: (1) **The Gen 1 creation-goodness as type** — God's "very good" declaration over creation (Gen 1:31) is the OT type pointing forward to the new creation (Isa 65:18 — God creates Jerusalem to be "a joy" and her people "a gladness" — gi.lah); the created goodness of the first creation is the type of the consummated goodness of the new; (2) **Psa 45:7's oil of gladness** (sa.s.von) applied christologically in Heb 1:9 — the anointed king's gladness beyond his companions is the OT type for Christ's eschatological anointing; (3) **The makarismos typology** (Rom 4:6, 9 — Abraham's blessedness as the type of the justified person's blessedness declared apart from works) — the OT blessedness pattern (in M04-O-VCG-04) is the type for NT declarative righteousness; (4) **God's good promises** (Jos 21:45; Jer 29:10; 33:14) as types of the final fulfillment in Christ — every good promise not one of which has failed finds its ultimate Yes in Christ (2Cor 1:20).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All seven characteristics evidence typological use, with three major convergence points: (1) **Christological convergence at Psa 118:23** — "This is the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes" (quoted in Mat 21:42). This verse is the primary Wonder (Char 6) anchor and is simultaneously the most programmatic christological type-fulfilment in the cluster: the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is named with the Wonder vocabulary. The cluster's typological use of Wonder is thus the most directly christological; (2) **Christological convergence at Isa 53:10** — "It was the will of the Lord to crush him" (cha.phets). This is the most theologically charged Delight (Char 4) instance: divine sovereign Delight as the inner mechanism of atonement. It is also an Exultation (Char 1) anchor via the suffering-servant connection; (3) **Christological convergence at Heb 12:2** — "For the joy that was set before him endured the cross." This is the primary Suffering-Joy (Char 7) type-fulfilment and simultaneously deploys the Joy (Char 2) vocabulary. Additional cluster-wide typological patterns: the OT feast-joy (Deu 16:11–15) is the type for the eschatological banquet (Mat 25:21; Rev 19:7); the Exodus wonders are the type for NT signs; the sa.s.von restoration-joy corpus is the type for the NT gospel joy; the cultic ni.cho.ach system is the type for Christ's self-offering (Eph 5:2). The cluster as a whole forms a typological arch from creation (Char 3's Gen 1 goodness) through Exodus (Char 6's wonder-wonders) through Zec 9:9 (Char 1's commanded exultation at the coming king) through Isa 9:6 (Char 6's Wonderful Counselor) through Isa 53:10 (Char 4's atonement-Delight) to Heb 12:2 (Char 7's cross-Joy) to eschatological fullness.

Partial evidence. The volitional-preference idiom (632-003) and the goodness-outcome blessing (542-001 — Deu 5:33) carry covenantal typology: the person who does well and receives blessing anticipates the fullness of covenant relationship. However, the M39-B verse set does not contain a developed christological typology for the goodness characteristic in the way M39-A does for blessing/grace.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — the Ninevites' repentance as a condemnation of unrepentant Israel (Mat 12:41–42; Luk 11:31–32, VSG 4846-001) is typological: a past generation's response to less light condemns a present generation's response to greater light.
